chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Hasan ibn Ali, from a man named Sawadah, who said:

We were a group in Mina, and the sacrificial animals became expensive for us, so we looked and saw Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) standing by a flock, bargaining with the sheep and haggling intensely. We stopped to watch, and when he finished, he turned to us and said, 'I think you were surprised by my haggling.' We said, 'Yes.' He said, 'The one who is overcharged is neither praiseworthy nor rewarded. Do you have a need?' We said, 'Yes, may Allah improve you, the sacrificial animals have become expensive for us.'

He said, 'So gather together and buy a camel, and slaughter it among yourselves.' We said, 'Our funds will not suffice for that.' He said, 'So gather together and buy a cow, and [slaughter] it among yourselves.' We said, 'Then our funds will not suffice for that.' He said, 'So gather together and buy a sheep, and slaughter it among yourselves.' We said, 'Does it suffice for seven?' He said, 'Yes, and for seventy.'

key_terms.الْمَغْبُونُ: The one who is overcharged/deceived in trade

ai.seo_question: Can multiple people share one sheep for Eid al-Adha sacrifice according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights Imam al-Sadiq’s (peace be upon him) practical approach to communal worship, where he validates the permissibility of sharing a single sacrificial animal among seven individuals to ease financial burden. The narrative begins with his intense bargaining (*mikas*), illustrating that commercial negotiation is a neutral act devoid of inherent blame or reward, before transitioning to the specific juristic ruling that a sheep suffices for seven people. This establishes a foundational precedent for *qurbani* sharing in Shia fiqh, emphasizing accessibility and communal solidarity during Hajj.
